title: Boolean blocks and the weak Lefschetz property of whiskered and chordal graph algebras
shortTitle: A proof of the whiskered-graph Lefschetz conjecture
oneLine: One change of variables splits the algebra into Boolean blocks, settling the Holleben-Nicklasson conjecture over every field and giving a Lefschetz criterion for all chordal graphs.
abstract: Take a graph, make one variable per vertex, and set every square and the product of any two adjacent vertices to zero; the resulting algebra records the graph's independent sets. The weak Lefschetz property asks whether multiplication by the sum of the variables has maximal rank in every degree. Holleben and Nicklasson (Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra, 2026) conjectured that the whiskered graph of G never has this property once G has three pairwise non-adjacent vertices; computer checks covered up to seven vertices, and an eight-vertex check was posted. This candidate proves the conjecture over every field and classifies exactly when the weak and strong properties hold: for G with n vertices, the weak property needs G complete, or n odd with independence number two, and characteristic zero or larger than about n/2; the strong property holds only for complete graphs. The same classification is given for Holleben and Nicklasson's Gorenstein algebras, and a criterion for both properties is given for every chordal graph in every characteristic, recovering the path and lollipop classifications with short proofs. The key step is one change of variables that splits the algebra into Boolean blocks, one per independent set; Wilson's diagonal form of inclusion matrices gives every rank. Limits: the method needs a private leaf at every vertex or removable simplicial vertices, so cycles and tadpole graphs are not covered, and prime thresholds for unequal higher exponents are open. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

evidence: A 13-page paper with a plain introduction (the problem, what was known, Theorems A to C, the key idea and a roadmap) and written proofs of every theorem. Two Python programs accompany it: verify.py builds the multiplication matrices in the original variables and compares exact ranks over prime fields with the theorems (75 whiskered graphs with 8,440 rank comparisons, a non-flag complex, 894 chordal graphs with 18,680 comparisons, higher exponents and the eight-vertex example with rank 386 between dimensions 400 and 406); chordal_lefschetz.py uses exact integer arithmetic for 1,128 direct eliminations against the block profiles and reproduces the path and lollipop lists and prime thresholds. A clean replay reproduced both recorded outputs byte for byte in Python's optimised mode; changing the published path list or the weak-property threshold makes the scripts fail; Linux CI reruns both and compares outputs exactly. The computations accompany the written proofs; they do not replace them.

keyResults: Theorem A (proof): the whiskered-graph algebra of G has the weak Lefschetz property if and only if the independence number is at most 1 for even n or at most 2 for odd n, and the characteristic is zero or exceeds ceil(n/2); it has the strong property if and only if G is complete and the characteristic is zero or exceeds n. This proves the Holleben–Nicklasson conjecture over every field.

Section 3 (proof): after the change of variables y_i -> x_i + y_i, multiplication by the sum of the variables is a direct sum of shifted Boolean operators, one per independent set; Wilson's diagonal form gives every rank in every characteristic. Example: for K8 minus a triangle, A4 -> A5 has rank 386 between dimensions 400 and 406.

Theorem B (proof): the same classification, with thresholds ceil((n+1)/2) and n+1, for the Nagata idealisation, which is Holleben and Nicklasson's G-quadratic Perazzo algebra for non-complete G in characteristic zero.

Theorem C (proof): for chordal graphs, eliminating simplicial vertices splits the algebra into Boolean blocks; the weak and strong properties depend only on the block types, with explicit prime thresholds.

Corollaries 7.5 and 7.6 (proof with a finite exact check): paths have the weak property exactly for 1-7, 9, 10 and 13 vertices and the strong property for 1-7 and 9, with prime thresholds; the lollipop lists likewise, in every characteristic.

Credit and limits: Holleben–Nicklasson Lemma 3.1 contains the complete-graph case of the splitting and their Theorem 4.6 the projection argument used for Theorem B. Cycles, tadpole graphs and very well-covered graphs in general are not covered; prime thresholds for unequal higher exponents are open.
